text:
Here's the LLM design prompt in its usual form: an assistant that answers questions from a company's documents, and can file a support ticket. It's fast now, and cheap. Is it any good? A classifier has one right label per example. This has many good answers to every question, and more bad ones, so measuring it is a design problem of its own. Six questions.

Question one. How do you evaluate an LLM application? In layers, from cheap to expensive. First, an offline eval set: realistic inputs, each with a reference answer or a rubric. A hundred or two well-chosen cases beat thousands of synthetic ones, and the set grows from real production failures. Second, scoring matched to the task: exact match or execution for structured output like jay-son, sequel or code, retrieval metrics for search, and a rubric-driven LLM judge for open-ended text. For the assistant, whether a ticket was filed with the right fields can be checked exactly. Whether it explained a policy correctly needs the judge. Third, human review of a sample, to catch what the metrics miss and to check the judge. Fourth, evals as CI: rerun the suite on every prompt, model or retrieval change, and block regressions. Fifth, online: A B tests on user outcomes, with guardrails on latency, cost and refusal rate. The layers have to agree. When a change wins offline and loses online, fix the eval set: it's measuring something users don't care about. And public benchmarks are a weak guide to your task: many are saturated, and their test items may have leaked into training data. Several of those layers lean on an LLM judge, so the judge comes next.
